title: Legal Analysis
subtitle: Not a neutral briefing, but a record of where the case breaks with law, evidence, and elementary legal logic.
intro: This section is the legal backbone of the defence. It shows the architecture of the arbitrariness in plain view: a commercial transaction upheld as lawful in arbitration is repackaged as fraud; a lawyer's professional work is repackaged as participation in a criminal scheme; and the investigators' own records are read against their own text.

sections.title: Defence in Serbia (Extradition Proceedings)
sections.content: Procedural submissions and memoranda filed before Belgrade courts.
sections.summary: The defence has consistently established that the extradition request is grounded in a transaction whose lawfulness has been confirmed by arbitration. This is the legal barrier against an attempt to criminalise a civil commercial relationship.

sections.title: Human Rights Dimension
sections.content: Findings and positions of independent institutions on the risks of arbitrary prosecution.
sections.summary: The case has been characterised as one that violates basic fair-trial standards. Human rights practitioners document the disproportionality of the criminal pressure and point to the instrumentalisation of law enforcement in a private corporate dispute.

sections.title: Independent Legal Expertise
sections.content: Analytical notes, expert opinions, and memoranda from international law practitioners.
sections.summary: A detailed unpacking of the legal contradictions in this case. Experts examine the absence of a criminal offence, the collapse of the conspiracy theory, and the legal consequences of disregarding binding arbitration rulings in criminal proceedings.

sections.title: Evidence Turned on Its Head: How the Investigators Read Their Own Records
sections.content: An analysis of three key episodes from inspection records (December 2022, November 2023) where the investigators reach conclusions that are the direct opposite of what those same records actually say.

episodes.label: 'The value must be real' — treated as proof of a conspiracy to suppress value
episodes.what_protocol_says: CRM message, 01.12.2021, 10:11: Lagovsky D. V. writes to Osipova M. V. — 'the value must be real.' The inspection record (17.12.2022) quotes this phrase verbatim and characterises it as evidence that the parties agreed to an undervalued appraisal.
episodes.what_it_actually_means: 'Real value' means market value. Someone trying to get a deflated appraisal writes 'give us a lower number' — not 'the value must be real.' The phrase is the exact opposite of what the investigators infer from it. If there had been a conspiracy to suppress value, this very phrase would be the strongest evidence against the investigators' theory.

episodes.label: A 'pointless' trip to collect the report — treated as evidence of criminal intent
episodes.what_protocol_says: The inspection record (17.12.2022) characterises Lagovsky's visit to the offices of LLC 'Company for Valuation and Law' on 14.07.2021 to collect the original of report No. 2021/447 as 'illogical and not justified by his duties' — and draws from this a conclusion about criminal intent.
episodes.what_it_actually_means: From the very same CRM correspondence quoted in that same record, it is clear that the original of report No. 2021/447 had been sent to Lagovsky by post back in April 2021. The July visit was a follow-up request for a physical copy, directly documented in the correspondence. The 'illogicality' of the trip is explained in the very materials the investigators cite as evidence.

episodes.label: 'Ira, thanks, sent in PDF' — treated as proof of conspiracy with the appraiser
episodes.what_protocol_says: The inspection record (November 2023, Sorokina's phone) quotes a WhatsApp exchange among management at LLC 'KOP'. Sorokina I. O.'s reply 'Ira, thanks, sent in PDF' is included in the body of facts which, according to the investigators, 'indicate that KOP employees agreed to produce a report with an understated value'.
episodes.what_it_actually_means: 'Sent in PDF' is a routine office acknowledgement that a finished document has been forwarded. This is the kind of message you would find in the correspondence of any appraisal firm in any country. Neither this message nor its context contains a word about suppressing value, about a deal with the client, or about any departure from professional standards.

sections.summary: All three episodes share one feature: the investigators quote their documents accurately, then interpret them in a direction diametrically opposed to the plain meaning of what is written. This is not a reading error — it is a systemic approach. Readers can verify this themselves: the source documents are publicly available.

summary: This section presents the consolidated position of leading legal experts. It brings together the arguments for returning this case to the rule of law and ending a prosecution that lacks any legitimate legal basis.

theses.title: Defending the Legal Profession: UN Principles
theses.text: The prosecution of Dmitry Lagovsky is a direct assault on the independence of the legal profession. Under the UN Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers, lawyers must not be identified with their clients or their clients' causes as a result of carrying out their professional duties. By seeking to extradite a lawyer for professional advice on compliance with market standards, Serbia sets a dangerous precedent: any lawyer anywhere in the world can now be arrested at a foreign government's request simply for doing their job in good faith. This is the complete destruction of legal certainty. If a professional opinion can constitute a criminal offence, law as an institution ceases to function.
theses.source: UN Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers (1990), Principle 18

sources.label: UN Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers, Principle 18

theses.title: Corporate Conflict and the Weaponisation of Criminal Law
theses.text: This is a textbook example of how a local corporate dispute — one that a minority shareholder lost comprehensively in the highest arbitration courts — gets artificially converted into a criminal matter. The criminal case is being used here not to enforce the law but as a weapon of retaliation and leverage in a private commercial conflict. The lawyer was chosen as the most convenient target — a 'procedural hostage' whose prosecution is designed to paralyse the company's legal defence. The Serbian courts' failure to engage with the arbitration rulings and Supreme Court judgments that confirmed the lawfulness of the transaction is a critical failure of the judicial filter that extradition proceedings are supposed to apply.
theses.source: Russian arbitration and Supreme Court rulings, 2024–2025

theses.title: The Absurdity of the Charge: Res Judicata and the Actual Sentences Handed Down
theses.text: The charges against Lagovsky rest on the alleged 'undervaluation' of a transaction that the Supreme Court of the requesting state has officially found to be at market value and lawful. Moreover, the main defendants in the case — the company directors and owners — have already received suspended sentences of 1 year and 10 months in Russia. Against this backdrop, the demand to extradite a legal consultant in order to remand him in pre-trial custody is an act of manifest legal arbitrariness. Extradition-related detention and removal in a case that the requesting state itself regards as not warranting imprisonment for the principal organisers violate the principle of proportionality and Articles 5 and 6 of the ECHR.
